title: Cluster 01 DRILL: Variation, Natural Selection and the Evidence for Evolution
subtitle: H2 Biology 9477 · Book 7 · 8 questions · 81 marks · 24 parts · one mark per minute, so a little over an hour and a quarter · every question is an actual exam paper question
los_html:
Learning outcomes, against the questions that test them.
4(a) why variation is important in natural selectionQ1(a), Q1(d), Q3(a)
4(a) the three named sources: mutation, meiosis, sexual reproductionQ1(b), Q1(c), Q8
4(b) environmental factors as forces of selection, with examplesQ3(a) competition, Q3(b) temperature, Q3(c) dissolved oxygen, Q3(d) an antibiotic, Q4
4(b) / 4(c) the three curve shapes and what produces eachQ3(c), Q4
4(c) natural selection defined, and evolution as allele frequency changeQ2(a), Q2(b), Q2(c), Q3(d), Q4, Q8
4(c) selection acts on pre-existing variation, not on variation the environment madeQ2(b), Q3(d), Q4, Q8
4(g) anatomical homologies and the pentadactyl limbQ5, Q6(a), Q7(a)
4(g) analogy and convergent evolutionQ6(b), Q6(c)
4(g) molecular homologies and the accumulation argumentQ5
4(g) the fossil record: what it shows and why fossils are rareQ6(c), Q7(a), Q7(b), Q7(c), Q7(d)
4(g) biogeography, supported by Wallace's findingsQ2(d), Q6(c), Q7(e)
4(f) descent with modification as the conclusion lineQ2(a), Q5, Q7(d), Q7(e)
bridge to 4(j) which mode of selection can split a gene poolQ4
reach-back 2(k) gene mutation and chromosomal aberration (Book 2)Q1(b)
reach-back 2(a) semi-conservative replication (Book 2)Q8
reach-back 2(s), 2(t) crossing over, independent assortment, random fertilisation (Book 3)Q1(b), Q8
reach-back horizontal gene transfer: transformation, transduction, conjugation (Book 4)Q3(d), Q8

One primary concept each, checked for duplicated required answers as well as duplicated labels. Q1 what variation is for and where it comes from · Q2 what natural selection is, run on a bird the notes never mention · Q3 four different environmental factors acting as four different selection pressures · Q4 the three modes set out in full, and the one that can split a gene pool · Q5 homology as evidence, anatomical and molecular, at essay length · Q6 similarity that is not ancestry · Q7 the fossil record and biogeography, including what each cannot show · Q8 the whole cycle from new allele to changed frequency, twice over. The modes of selection are set out once, in Q4, and nothing else in the set repeats them. The pentadactyl limb is argued once, in Q5, and Q6(a) only asks you to read a limb plan off a figure. The single shared marking point in the set is random fusion of gametes, which Q1(b) needs as a source of variation and Q8 needs as a route of transmission; the two schemes score it for different reasons, so the answers do not collapse into each other.

Nothing from Cluster 2 or Cluster 3, and nothing from Books 8 or 9. Genetic drift, gene flow, the founder and bottleneck effects, heterozygote advantage, sickle cell and the whole of Hardy-Weinberg are Cluster 2, so no question here needs them. The species concept, speciation, phylogenetic trees and multiple sequence alignment are Cluster 3. Question 4 reaches forward to name the isolation categories only because its own mark scheme does.
